research.name: Reference board
research.what: Watched the openings, layouts and endings of 54 shows to find what makes a remote show feel designed.

findings.title: Cold open first, show title second.
findings.body: Most episodes open on a cold open before any title, usually 30 to 60 seconds long. Among shows that run a title in the first three minutes, it lands at a median of 0:33. The outliers (DOAC, Colin and Samir, Lenny's at 1:40 to 2:06) have audiences who came for a famous guest; ours come for the promise in the title.

findings.title: The promise goes on screen before the content.
findings.body: The strongest shows close the cold open with a roadmap, checklist or 'In this episode' agenda in the title's own words, then bring it back as the recap. Open Residency, the one channel that clearly outperforms on edit and packaging, does exactly this and delivers what its titles promise.

findings.title: Captions belong to the cold open.
findings.body: Kinetic captions sell the opening and then stop. The conversation runs clean. The common treatment is one phrase at a time beside the speaker, one keyword in the accent color, and the host's lines in a second color so viewers know who is asking.

findings.title: One canvas and one accent make any webcam look like the show.
findings.body: Remote shows hold mismatched home webcams together with a shared surface (a brand-color frame, bordered cards on one background, outlined panels) and one accent color repeated on every graphic that touches the webcam.

findings.title: Screens are never shown raw.
findings.body: The demo shows use three layouts and pick by how dense the screen is: a screen card beside the webcams (default), a full-frame screen with a small corner or circle cam (dense pages), and a punch-in on the one button, number or prompt (single actions). Phones get a phone frame; typed commands can get a keystroke overlay.

findings.title: Proof is an object with a source.
findings.body: Claims become things on screen: a screenshot on a card with a source line, the key sentence highlighted, one big number stamped when the guest says it, the guest's own post with its view count. The best shows label what is real ('REAL FOOTAGE', 'SOURCE').

findings.title: Plain-language helpers carry non-technical viewers.
findings.body: Definition cards the moment a guest says jargon, a context bar that explains a term, a photo tile for any person or tool mentioned, and the host's questions on screen as labels. This is the cheapest way to serve 'AI belongs to everyone'.

findings.title: Guests are introduced fast, with a credential and a receipt.
findings.body: A name card inside the cold open or a lower third timed to the second the guest says their name, a credential a viewer recognizes, and one receipt (their post, their product, their result) within seconds.

findings.title: Sponsors and asks are marked and timed.
findings.body: Reads come after the hook, never before the title, and carry a progress bar, an ad badge with an emptying ring, or a 'Presented by' badge. Owned opt-ins work best tied to what is on screen (the prompt, the playbook) and repeated at the close.

findings.title: Endings hand off to the guest or a next step.
findings.body: Instead of long outros, the strongest endings recap the promise, give one thing to do next, and put the guest's site or offer on screen, which gives guests a reason to share. A single reusable outro carries the show identity.

findings.title: The parent brand stays small.
findings.body: Successful shows under a parent keep their own name, color and look, and credit the parent in one quiet place: a line under the sting, a corner bug, or an end-card slot.

findings.title: Thumbnails: one face, a few words.
findings.body: Most thumbnails lead with one face and four to six words, and half highlight a single word. For a show about what people built, Starter Story's version is the model: the guest holding the thing they made.

research.name: Design research
research.what: Studied 26 of the most popular video podcasts and design-led explainers for identity systems.

findings.title: In a remote show, the frame around the feeds is the set
findings.body: New Heights is recorded from two homes and is still identifiable before you see the Kelces, because every tile has the same green field, cream stroke and corner radius. Good Hang keylines every Zoom feed inside its triangle pattern, Vox's The Gray Area uses two rounded tiles on one pastel field, and Pivot and Decoder make two home offices one show with a single rule and a corner plate. None of them design per episode; they pick four or five layouts and reuse them.

findings.title: One color or gesture, rationed to one job
findings.body: Mel Robbins puts one yellow highlighter swipe on the logo, the mic cube, the thumbnails and the one sentence that matters on a book page. Vox keeps yellow for the single thing to look at, Decoder's acid lime only labels or points, and Veritasium spends red on two things only: the human for scale and the headline underline. Because the color is rare, viewers learn to follow it.

findings.title: The brand lives on an object in the room
findings.body: Call Her Daddy's red cube mic flag and Mel's white cube put the logo in nearly every shot at no edit cost. Ezra Klein carries red NYT mugs onto every location, Good Hang has a neon sign and a laptop sticker in the raw host camera, The Gray Area hangs its wordmark as a print behind the host, and Shawn Ryan reads each guest intro from a card printed with the wordmark. Pivot gets the same effect from one red chair in a home office.

findings.title: A mark simple enough to be a symbol
findings.body: Rich Roll's circle with a slash works on a mic end cap, the center of a QR code and the sting, and it already reads like an engineering diameter symbol. Dive Club's 'd' is also a diver, Veritasium's element tile becomes data tiles and a shelf prop, and Practical Engineering's hard hat and glasses turn into a mannequin inside the diagrams. Each mark means something without the wordmark next to it.

findings.title: Drafting notation reads to general audiences
findings.body: Branch Education (2.8M subscribers) labels everything with hairline leader lines that end in a ring on the part. Real Engineering (5.1M) names views and dimensions angles, The B1M (4.1M) puts every graphic on one dark drafting grid, and Practical Engineering (4.8M) zooms in with a detail box and projection cone. Veritasium (21M) draws dimension marks over real footage. None of these audiences are engineers, and the notation makes the explanation feel exact without extra text.

findings.title: Every piece of proof gets the same container and a source line
findings.body: Ezra Klein treats a remote webcam clip exactly like archival footage, a rounded inset on charcoal with a credit, so low-quality video looks deliberate. Kurzgesagt recolors real browser windows around articles, Decoder tags every borrowed clip with a mono source chip, and PolyMatter gives every table a Source line. A messy screen becomes evidence once it is framed and credited.

findings.title: Rituals with their own graphic
findings.body: Every Conan guest opens with the same fill-in sentence, so the first five seconds identify the show by ear. Ezra Klein ends every episode with book recommendations that build up as cards, Mel Robbins shows listener questions as cards signed with a first name, and Johnny Harris moves a marker along a five-slot tray as the argument progresses. A repeated beat with a fixed graphic gives every episode the same shape.

findings.title: A locked thumbnail with one variable
findings.body: Jay Shetty, Shawn Ryan and Call Her Daddy change only the guest and the headline, so the channel page reads as one series. Dive Club keeps its layout and changes one accent color per guest, and New Heights runs a header row with a full-width rule like the top of a printed sheet. The celebrity shows lead with the guest's name; the shows with unknown guests lead with a claim the viewer wants.

findings.title: Sub-formats change the world and keep the frame
findings.body: New Heights' film breakdown, Tape Time, swaps the green field for a chalkboard margin full of play marks but keeps the stroked tile and the bug. Armchair Expert's Mom's Car gets a full retro print-ad identity, and Call Her Daddy's Sunday Sessions moves to a library set with the same mic flag. This is also the model for AIS Media as a parent of several shows.

research.what: Collected how 23 of the biggest shows end episodes and turned the patterns into templates.

findings.title: Every show that has a designed ending used the identical one in both sampled episodes. It is built once and reused.
The designed part runs 10 to 24 seconds, most often 16 to 20, which matches YouTube's 20-second end-screen limit.
Pointing at the click is the most common device: five shows have the host point or say 'watch this next', and three more draw arrows or labels at the elements.

stages.name: Ingest
stages.what: Pulls the raw recording into a project folder and transcribes it word by word so every later agent can cut on exact timestamps.

stages.name: Cut silences
stages.output: Silence EDL, re-timed transcript, silenced MP4
stages.what: Agent 1 of the video editing pipeline. Removes silences and dead air from a talking-head recording. Use when asked to cut silences, trim pauses, remove dead air / gaps, or tighten the pacing of a raw video, given a word-level transcript. Produces an edit list (EDL), a re-timed transcript for downstream agents, and optionally the cut video via ffmpeg. Does NOT cut mistakes, repeats, or false starts, that is the cut-mistakes agent.

stages.name: Cut mistakes
stages.what: Agent 2 of the video editing pipeline. Finds and removes spoken mistakes, stutters, repeated words, false starts, and retakes (re-recorded lines), from a talking-head recording. Use after cut-silences, when asked to cut mistakes, remove stutters / repeats / filler restarts, clean up flubs, or keep the best take. Works review-gated: it proposes every cut with context and a reason for approval, then renders only the approved cuts via ffmpeg. Requires a word-level transcript.

stages.name: Verify cuts
stages.output: Fresh transcript, verify report with PASS
stages.what: The passing agent (Agent 2.5) of the video editing pipeline. A verification-only step run after cut-silences and cut-mistakes have rendered, it re-transcribes the rendered video and makes AT LEAST THREE full passes through the script/transcript to verify every silence and every approved cut actually landed. Use when asked to verify an edit, run the passing agent, check the cuts, confirm silences are gone, or sign off a clean render. It never edits video itself; failures route back to cut-silences / cut-mistakes.

stages.name: Motion graphics
stages.gate: Gate 1: approve the beat plan and Studio preview
stages.what: Agent 3 of the video editing pipeline. Adds tiered motion-graphic cards (tier-1 full-screen takeovers for theses/stats/overviews, tier-2 glass lower-thirds and labels) over a clean talking-head edit, pulling distinct templates from the style-library card pool. Use after cut-silences + cut-mistakes, when asked to add motion graphics, beats, callouts, lower-thirds, stat cards, section takeovers, or "make it look edited / editorial-style / premium". Review-gated: proposes a beat plan from the transcript, you approve + write the on-card text, then it selects cards from the library and assembles one render-ready index.html. Requires a word-level transcript + the clean video.

stages.name: B-roll
stages.what: Agent 4 of the video editing pipeline. Inserts b-roll and visual assets (stock clips, photos, tool/brand logos, live website screenshots) over a clean talking-head edit, as cutaways (full-frame, narration continues) or overlays (speaker stays visible). Pulls from a local asset database (asset-library/) and free web providers (Pexels, Pixabay, Unsplash, Openverse, Wikimedia, Clearbit/Simple Icons logos, local Playwright screenshots, Firecrawl), caching every fetch back into the library. Use after motion-graphics, when asked to add b-roll, cutaways, visuals, screenshots of a tool/site, stock footage, or logos. Review-gated: detects visual moments from the transcript, you confirm + pick/fetch assets, then it comps them in. Requires a word-level transcript + the clean video.

stages.name: Render
stages.what: Renders a draft, pulls one hero frame per beat for visual QA, then renders the final after Gate 2.

orchestrator.name: edit-talking-head-video
orchestrator.what: Orchestrate the complete local, transcript-driven talking-head video pipeline: ingest and transcribe raw media, cut silences, review and cut spoken mistakes, review and add motion graphics, review and insert b-roll, validate, preview, and render. Use when asked to edit a raw talking-head video end to end, run the full video pipeline, resume a partially completed edit, or produce a polished final video from a recording. Invokes the project-local stage skills sequentially and preserves every review gate.
